section_1_unit_metadata.essay_title: Introduction: Being-Moved: The Pathos of Heidegger's Rhetorical Ontology
section_1_unit_metadata.sub_unit_label: Section IV 'The Priority of Pathos' + 49 Notes
section_1_unit_metadata.author: Daniel M. Gross
section_1_unit_metadata.essay_thesis: In Heidegger's 1924 reading of Aristotle's Rhetoric II, pathos is not an ancillary supplement to logos (the Roman compromise) nor a vice of psychology (the Christian and Enlightenment denigration), but the very ontological ground out of which logos springs forth and on which logos remains continuously suspended; this rhetorical-ontological priority is operative in Being and Time as Befindlichkeit, but Heidegger's post-1927 turn from rhetoric to hermeneutics (and the resulting depoliticization of language) is what leaves him without resources to think the political-rhetorical adequately, with consequences traceable into the 1933 Nazi turn.

section_2_hierarchical_outline.rhetorical_structure: Hybrid genealogical-philological argument culminating in political-philosophical critique. Section IV is a sustained argumentative arc with three structural movements: (a) historical-genealogical critique of the Roman/Christian denigration of pathos; (b) close reading of Heidegger's GA 18 (SS 1924) reading of Aristotle's Rhetoric II as ontological substrate; (c) political-philosophical denouement on Heidegger's 1933 turn as symptom of having lost rhetorical-political resources.
macro_arc: Bridge from end of Section III: Heidegger's 1924 treatment of pathos as 'turning point' (book p. 27, top, transitional paragraph closing Section III) — pathos no longer ancillary to rational discourse; pathos is the foundation of logos and social discourse

Section IV proper opens (book p. 27) with pathos's historical caution: Plato's anti-rhetorical discomfort, the Roman compromise (Cicero/Quintilian), Aristotle's own ambivalence in Rhetoric I vs. Rhetoric II

Roman tradition section (book pp. 28-29): Cicero De inventione, De oratore (Antonius); Quintilian Institutio oratoria 6.1.7; pathos added to logos 'by sheer fiat' as a posteriori contingent compromise

Survey of contemporary apologetic readings (book p. 29-30, the Engberg-Pedersen footnote 45 in Rorty's anthology) — Aristotle himself participates in the denigration in Rhetoric I.1 (1354a) — but BUT in Rhetoric II Aristotle gives a 'very different Aristotle' for whom pathē are the very condition of judgment (krisis); GA 18 169 quote

The doxa-pathos cell (book pp. 30-32): doxa as 'pretheoretical being-for' (GA 18 149); Ja-sagen / yes-saying without examination (GA 18 136-137); doxa 'could be otherwise' (Es könnte auch anders sein); doxa is set out as 'the ground and motive for speaking-with-one-another, negotiating-with-one-another' (GA 18 151) — pathos is the negotiation latent in doxa

Limits-of-the-human passage (book p. 33): 'It is precisely our limits that make us human (not God or simple animal) and motivate us to eloquence' — moving and persuading is itself an essential human activity

The Christian-theological genealogy of Affektenlehre (book pp. 33-34): Augustine (De civitate Dei, Pelagianische Schriften), Damascenus (De fide orthodoxa II), Gregory of Nyssa, Nemesius, pseudo-Dionysius Areopagita, Dilthey's Weltanschauung text — but the project to be undertaken here is narrower: 'the impact of one central tenet on Heidegger's rhetorical philosophy: pathos alone has the power to provide logos with a critical moment, kairos'

Luther's Affektenlehre (book p. 34, footnote 47, 48): the rhetorical mastery of Klaus Dockhorn; Luther grounds Enlightenment philosophy by enabling the 'hermeneutics of facticity' (Heidegger and Gadamer); 'Belief realizes itself in affect — must complete itself in affect — because reason is incapable of making past and future present' (Dockhorn citing Luther's Tischreden 'Dialectica docet, Rhetorica movet')

Heidegger's analysis of fear (phobos) — book pp. 34-37 (GA 18 §§ on fear): SS 1924 review of how logos and doxa 'can be bound by way of fear'; community and its Other are defined; we ask 'What is to be done?'; the fearsome situation is composed in immediacy (kairos) by concrete possibilities, not by phantasia

Quintilian 6.2.29 phantasia citation contrasted with Heidegger (book p. 34): the Roman fantasy of phantasia as the engine of rhetorical performance; Heidegger reverses this — individual mentation is product of passion, not its source

Three states of nonhuman being (book p. 35): dog (no belief), dogmatist (belief but not subject-to-change), Descartes (perfectly rational but disembodied). Pathos gives Being its dynamism; pathos = uncertainty, 'unsettling' (Unruhe), 'confusing' (Verwirrung), 'mixed-up' (Durcheinandergeraten) [GA 18 183]

The pathos-as-Umschlagen quote (book pp. 35-36): GA 18 171 — 'Pathos is a sudden change and hence a transformation to ... out of a previous situation'; hexis; being-suddenly-overcome; being-composed-for [Gefaßtsein dafür]

Logos-Pathos consequence summary (book p. 36): without pathos no traffic between inside and outside, self and Other, individual and community; pathos is what makes us subject-to-movement; without pathos we would be deaf, blind, mute and apathetic; living without pathos would be 'poisonous to our collective well-being'

Pathos = krisis/kairos/Dafürsein — book pp. 36-37 (GA 18 259, 256-257): pathos folds past experience and future possibilities into a provisional present; the 'Being-there-for' (Dafürsein); the relational aspect of fear (afraid OF someone who could harm me); Aristotle's typology (Rhet 1382a30 area) of nine kinds of fearsome people grouped under three categories ('ill disposed' / 'always seeking advantage' / 'cowardly')

Mögliche-Bezug-zur-hexis passage (book p. 37, GA 18 253): possibility (Möglichkeit) as the structural feature of fear; the most fearsome are those most 'reserved' (Zurückhaltenden) and 'ironic' (Ironischen) [GA 18 257]

The genesis of language is pathos (book p. 37, GA 18 261): 'fear is precisely Befindlichkeit that brings into speech' (die zum Sprechen bringt); 'die daseinsmäßige genesis des Sprechens'; pathos is the ground of logos — providing the mood and motivation necessary for the speaking animal

GA 18 262 long block-quote (book p. 38): how the pathē compose 'the ground upon which language grows and to which expressions return'; pathē provide 'the fundamental possibilities in which Dasein finds itself and orients itself'; finding-oneself rather than knowledge; Sachlichkeit as how the world is prefigured by the pathē

Tilde-ornament transition (book p. 39 — section structurally turns to political consequences): 'Whatever happened to this more agreeable Heidegger who seemed at one time to be working on the very sort of pluralism Arendt would later characterize as the antidote to Heideggerian politics?'

Heidegger 1930s on Nietzsche (book p. 39): a long Heidegger quote on 'Affect' vs. 'Passion' and great will / great passion (citing Heidegger Nietzsche I 48-49) — passion 'displays the self-composed superiority characteristic of great will' [italics added by Gross]

Body politic subordinated to great will (book p. 39, end of p. 39 - top of p. 40): Heidegger's 1933 speeches (resolute Freeman → resolute nation, French rationalism, American cultural imperialism, German withdrawal from League of Nations, adherence to the German Führer) — far cry from rhetorical pluralism of 1924

The 1924-pluralist-Heidegger thesis (book pp. 40-41, GA 18 127): 'The determination of Being-with-one-another in politikē founds that which rhetoric brings to language' [GA 18 127]; humans have political existence (bios politikos) only as actions are coordinated in a common world; ethics shows how Being-in-the-world is differentiated, and rhetoric how Dasein's articulations are situated in time and place

BT-as-rupture passage (book p. 40): in BT, suspicion of das Man and sociality grew while authentic Being-with withered; BT 238 — ethics reconstructed via care-as-totality, primordial phenomena reach above factical situations; BT 344 — only authentically being-their-Selves in resoluteness can people authentically be with one another; BT 159 — half-hearted suggestion that people can be authentically bound when devoted to 'the same affair in common'; BT 434 — Heidegger has already moved out of emotional public sphere into rarefied domain of resolute Freeman

Closing thesis (book p. 41): SS 1924 marks the rhetorical turn AND the revision of the rhetorical tradition that depoliticizes it; rhetoric absorbed into 'fallen' discourse and poetic speech-acts; rhetorical responsibility for what one did/changed in the world handed to logicians (legalities) and grammarians (locutions); Grice/Searle/Habermas/Sperber take over the illocutionary/perlocutionary analysis as 'background of unarticulated predispositions' — depoliticization complete; ironic punchline: 'Martin Heidegger's early work on Aristotle's rhetoric allows us to reconsider how political, ethical, and emotional context is in fact constitutive of everyday language'

Notes (book pp. 41-45): 49 numbered end-of-chapter footnotes — primary loci anchors in notes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (GA 18 + Löwith + Kisiel Genesis); secondary literature in notes 8-23 (Dockhorn, Shuger, Van Buren, Gadamer, Schleiermacher); Christian/Roman tradition in notes 24-46 (Villa, Arendt, Kennedy, Rorty, Engberg-Pedersen, Garver); Lutheran-Affektenlehre in notes 47-48 (Dockhorn quoting Heidegger SS 1924 long German passage on pathē in Middle Ages); closing in note 49 (Heidegger Nietzsche I 48-49)

section_3_key_concepts.name: the priority of pathos
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Pathos is not added to logos as a Roman afterthought, nor is it the suspect psychological supplement Plato distrusts; rather (per Heidegger reading Aristotle Rhetoric II), pathos is what makes logos possible — 'the very substance in which propositional thought finds its objects and motivation' (forward-referenced from p. 4) — the ground out of which language grows and to which expressions return (GA 18 262).

section_3_key_concepts.name: Roman compromise (logos+pathos by sheer fiat)
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Cicero's and Quintilian's solution to the Platonic distrust of emotion: pathos is *added to* logos 'by sheer fiat' as an a posteriori, contingent pragmatic compromise — useful when arguing 'before real people' (Engberg-Pedersen) but optionally droppable when no mass audience is involved. The compromise leaves logos with a monopoly on the prestige of truth and treats pathos as 'regrettably necessary.' Heidegger explicitly rejects this compromise.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Affektenlehre (doctrine of affections)
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: doctrine of affections / theological-rhetorical pathos tradition
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The Christian-theological transformation of Aristotle's pathē — running from Augustine, Damascenus, Gregory of Nyssa, pseudo-Dionysius, through medieval *Thomas' Affektenlehre*, to Luther — for whom emotion is what makes belief realize itself in affect; Dockhorn's claim is that Luther's Affektenlehre 'grounds Enlightenment philosophy' and opens 'the way for what would later become the hermeneutics of facticity practiced by both Heidegger and Gadamer.' Gross uses this as the genealogical bridge from Aristotle through Christian theology to Heidegger.

section_3_key_concepts.name: doxa as pretheoretical disposition / Dafürsein
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's reading of doxa (GA 18 149-151): not propositional belief but 'authentic being-with-one-another in the world' (eigentliche Entdecktheit des Miteinanderseins-in-der-Welt) — a 'protolinguistic disposition or nonreflective perspective' (Ansicht) of yes-saying without examination (Ja-sagen ... kein Untersuchen, Reflektieren), characterized by 'openness' (Offenheit) and the always-being-able-to-be-otherwise (Es könnte auch anders sein). Doxa is provisional, fixity-with-revisability — the ground from which speaking-with-one-another and negotiating-with-one-another emerge.

section_3_key_concepts.name: pathos as Umschlagen / Befindlichkeit-bringing-into-speech
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per Heidegger GA 18 171: 'Pathos is a sudden change [Umschlagen] and hence a transformation to ... [Werden zu] out of a previous situation, but not a sudden change that would take its own course; rather a way of disposing oneself toward the world that stands at the same time in a possible relation to hexis.' Pathos is essentially being-suddenly-overcome (being-seized, being-made-to-lose-composure), structurally containing within itself the possibility of being-composed-for (Gefaßtsein dafür) — i.e., it has the structure of disposition for/from the next moment. Per GA 18 261: pathos is precisely 'the Befindlichkeit that brings into speech' (die zum Sprechen bringt) — language has its 'daseinsmäßige genesis' in fear and pathos.

section_3_key_concepts.name: fear (phobos) as relational-temporal Befindlichkeit
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per Heidegger's GA 18 reading of Aristotle Rhetoric II.5 (1382a20-1382b3 area), fear is not generic terror about imagined damage but a concrete relational-temporal positioning: 'I fear these people not because I can imagine the damage they could do ... but rather because my concrete relationship to this person — past and present — positions me unfavorably with respect to his or her capacity to harm me in the near future' (GA 18 256-257). The structural feature is *Möglichkeit* / *Möglichsein* — 'die Möglichkeit, daß es kann' (GA 18 253). Hence the most fearsome are 'the reserved' (*Zurückhaltenden*) and 'the ironic' (*Ironischen*) — those whose harm-possibility is structurally indeterminate (GA 18 257).

section_3_key_concepts.name: logos has its daseinsmäßige genesis in pathos
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: GA 18 261 thesis: 'When we feel uncanny [unheimlich], we begin to talk; this is a hint that speech belongs to the fundamental determination of Dasein, which is characterized by uncanniness [Unheimlichkeit]' (Wenn uns unheimlich ist, fangen wir an zu reden ...). Pathos — and especially fear — is what brings logos out into the open; it is the ontological precondition for speaking-with-one-another rather than a stylistic accessory. Per GA 18 262, the pathē are 'the ground upon which language grows and to which expressions return.'

section_3_key_concepts.name: kairos / krisis as folding past and future into provisional present
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per Gross's reading of GA 18 §§ on phobos: 'It is rather a decisive moment (krisis) that folds past experience and future possibilities into a provisional present.' Pathos provides logos with this critical moment; it is what makes the rhetor's articulation immediate (kairos), not the Roman/Quintilian fantasy of phantasia. Gross binds *kairos* and *Augenblick* implicitly here without using the German term in this section.

section_3_key_concepts.name: phantasia as Roman vs. Aristotelian-Heideggerian critique
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Quintilian Inst. or. 6.2.29: 'things absent are presented to our imagination [phantasia] with such extreme vividness that they seem actually to be before our very eyes.' Quintilian uses phantasia to fuel the orator's emotional performance (e.g., the murder-scenario example, 6.2.31). Gross uses this to characterize the Roman tradition — passions as 'product of individual mentation,' phantasia as the engine of pathos. Heidegger reverses this: individual mentation is the product of passion, not its source; pathos is composed by 'concrete possibilities contoured by experience,' not by fantasy.

section_3_key_concepts.name: depoliticization-by-hermeneutics
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: depoliticization (of the rhetorical) by the hermeneutic turn
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: The volume's signature thesis: SS 1924 marked the rhetorical turn AND the revision of the rhetorical tradition that depoliticized it. Heidegger 'artfully coaxed elements of the rhetorical tradition from their ethical and political home to be incorporated in an account of "fallen" discourse and poetic speech acts.' Rhetorical theory's responsibility for understanding 'what one did in speaking and what changes in the world one could thereby effect' was handed off to logicians and grammarians; speech-act theory (Grice, Searle, Habermas, Sperber) takes over but with no political-ethical context — only an 'unevaluated background of unarticulated predispositions.' Power is swept into discursive backgrounds, rhetoric depoliticized.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Heidegger's 1933 turn (Nazism) as forgetting of the rhetorical-pluralist 1924
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: On Gross's reading: Heidegger's 1933 speeches and writings (Rectoral Address, withdrawal-from-League-of-Nations rhetoric, the 'resolute Freeman → resolute nation' progression, adherence to the German Führer) are 'a far cry from the rhetorical pluralism that characterized Heidegger's nascent political philosophy in 1924.' This is presented not as a contingent biographical lapse but as the political-philosophical *consequence* of Heidegger's having abandoned the rhetorical-political resources he discovered in SS 1924. The 1933 Heidegger has subordinated the body politic to 'the so-called great will' (citing Heidegger's 1930s Nietzsche reading on Affect vs. Passion).

section_3_key_concepts.name: BT 178 — rhetoric as 'first systematic hermeneutic of everydayness of Being-with-one-another'
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: Rhetoric as first systematic hermeneutic of everydayness
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Heidegger's BT footnote citation of Aristotle's Rhetoric (BT 178/H 138) is repeated near top of book p. 27 as the entry-point to the Section IV argument. Gross: 'As Heidegger states explicitly in Being and Time, the second book of Aristotle's Rhetoric "must be taken as the first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being with one another," and SS 1924 is where this discovery was made public for the first time.' This BT 178 endorsement is the volume's most-cited rhetoric-affirming Heidegger quote.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Befindlichkeit and the dropping of pathos in BT
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Befindlichkeit is the BT name for what GA 18 calls pathos. Gross argues these are not pure equivalents — there is a quiet conceptual concealment in BT: 'in taking this leap [to BT], Heidegger dropped his convictions that public speaking could authentically emerge from political community and that such an emergence would be motivated by pathos.' BT 344: only authentically being-their-Selves in resoluteness can people authentically be with one another; BT 159: half-hearted suggestion of authentic Being-with through 'devoting themselves to the same affair in common'; BT 434: Heidegger has moved into 'the rarefied domain of the resolute Freeman.' Hence VT5's ontological-substrate vs. cognitive-rhetorical-resource tension within Heidegger himself.

section_3_key_concepts.name: Sachlichkeit as world-prefigured-by-pathē
section_3_key_concepts.english_form: matter-of-factness / specific way of seeing the world
section_3_key_concepts.definition_in_essay: Per GA 18 262 (Gross's translation): 'we are presented with the possibility of coming to a particular matter-of-fact (Sachlichkeit) that, in a certain sense, returns to the way the world is seen as prefigured by the pathē.' This is Gross's strongest single statement of the rhetorical-ontological thesis: matter-of-factness *itself* is rhetorical; it is downstream of how the pathē have prefigured the world. Sachlichkeit ≠ a neutral pre-rhetorical foundation against which rhetoric distorts; Sachlichkeit IS rhetorical.

section_4_main_positions.claim: Pathos is not ancillary to logos (Roman compromise) nor a vice of psychology (Christian/Enlightenment denigration); pathos is the ontological ground of logos. Per Heidegger's reading of Aristotle Rhetoric II in GA 18, the pathē are 'the ground upon which language grows and to which expressions return,' providing 'the fundamental possibilities in which Dasein finds itself and orients itself' (GA 18 262). This is the volume's signature thesis: 'the priority of pathos.'
premises: Aristotle Rhetoric II treats pathē as condition of judgment (krisis), not ancillary embellishment (Rhet 1377b-1378a area)
Heidegger's SS 1924 reading of Rhetoric II foregrounds pathē in this Aristotelian-not-Roman key
Heidegger's analysis of phobos (GA 18 §§ on fear) shows logos and doxa 'can be bound by way of fear' — fear constitutes community and motivates judgment
BT 178 explicitly endorses Rhetoric II as 'first systematic hermeneutic of everydayness of Being-with-one-another'
Therefore pathos is not psychology but ontology
targets: Roman tradition (Cicero, Quintilian) — logos+pathos by sheer fiat
Christian/Enlightenment denigration of emotion (Engberg-Pedersen as exemplar)
Plato's Gorgias-style dismissal of pathos-rhetoric
Aristotle Rhetoric I.1 (1354a) where Aristotle himself participates in the denigration

section_4_main_positions.claim: Doxa is not propositional belief but pretheoretical being-for (Dafürsein) — 'authentic being-with-one-another in the world' (eigentliche Entdecktheit des Miteinanderseins-in-der-Welt) — characterized by yes-saying-without-examination, by openness (Offenheit), and by the always-being-able-to-be-otherwise (Es könnte auch anders sein); doxa is the ground and motive for speaking-with-one-another and negotiating-with-one-another (GA 18 149-151).
premises: GA 18 149: doxa = eigentliche Entdecktheit des Miteinanderseins-in-der-Welt
GA 18 136-137: 'Ja-sagen ... kein Untersuchen, Reflektieren' — yes-saying without examination
GA 18 137: 'Es könnte auch anders sein' — provisional openness as structural
GA 18 151: doxa as Boden, Quelle und Antrieb für das Miteinanderreden
Therefore doxa is rhetorical-ontological substrate, not propositional content
targets: Cognitive-propositional accounts of belief
The reading that takes doxa as opinion to be replaced by knowledge

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's analysis of fear (phobos) in GA 18 — drawing on Aristotle Rhetoric II.5 — shows fear as relational-temporal-possibility-structure: I fear someone not because I imagine the damage they could do but because my concrete past-present relationship to them positions me unfavorably with respect to their capacity to harm me in the near future. Fear's structural feature is Möglichkeit/Möglichsein (GA 18 253), and fear is the Befindlichkeit 'that brings into speech' (GA 18 261) — language has its daseinsmäßige genesis in this pathos.
premises: GA 18 256-257: fear as relational positioning, not imagined damage
GA 18 253: 'Es muß sich zeigen — die Möglichkeit, daß es kann' — possibility as fear's structure
GA 18 257: most fearsome = the Reserved (Zurückhaltenden) and Ironic (Ironischen)
GA 18 261: 'Wenn uns unheimlich ist, fangen wir an zu reden' — uncanniness brings speech
GA 18 261: 'das Sprechen zusammenhängt mit der Grundbestimmung des Daseins, die durch die Unheimlichkeit charakterisiert ist'
Therefore phobos is not just emotion but the existentiale-structural origin of speaking
targets: Quintilian Inst. or. 6.2.29 phantasia model — fear as imagination-driven
Roman tradition's individual-mentation-first model

section_4_main_positions.claim: Pathos is essentially Umschlagen — sudden change, transformation-to (Werden zu) out of a previous situation, but not autonomous; pathos is structurally a way of disposing oneself toward the world that stands in possible relation to hexis. Pathos contains within itself the possibility of being-composed-for (Gefaßtsein dafür) — i.e., it is structurally bivalent: being-overcome and being-able-to-recover-composure (GA 18 171).
premises: GA 18 171 long quote: Pathos = Umschlagen + Werden zu, mit möglichem Bezug zur hexis
Pathos contains both being-suddenly-overcome and the disposition-for being-composed-for
Hence pathos's relation to hexis: pathos is the dynamic-pole of which hexis is the settled-pole
Therefore pathos is essentially temporal-dynamic, not static state
targets: Static accounts of emotion as state
The Cartesian disembodied-rational ideal Gross spoofs in the 'three nonhuman states' passage (dog, dogmatist, Descartes)

section_4_main_positions.claim: Without pathos, there would be no traffic between inside and outside, self and Other, individual and community; pathos is what makes humans subject-to-movement (Sein in Bewegung); a world without pathos would be 'effectively deaf, blind, and mute' and 'poisonous to our collective well-being.' Pathos is therefore not optional rhetorical decoration but constitutive of human community itself.
premises: Pathos generates the dynamism of belief — without it doxa would remain frozen
Pathos provides 'selective traffic with an environment' for human community
Without pathos: no sympathies/antipathies, no community-defining emotion
Without pathos: no capacity to absorb past experience and future possibility (no historical-temporal community)
Therefore: pathos constitutes the social-political community as such
targets: Apolitical philosophical psychology
Theoretical-rationalist disembodied accounts of community

section_4_main_positions.claim: Luther's Affektenlehre (per Dockhorn) grounds Enlightenment philosophy and opens the way for Heidegger's and Gadamer's hermeneutics of facticity — Luther's principle 'Belief realizes itself in affect — must complete itself in affect — because reason is incapable of making past and future present' anticipates Heidegger's claim that pathos is what folds past and future into a provisional present (kairos). Heidegger's analysis of fear 'clearly draws on this Lutheran tradition while rewriting its residual metaphysics.'
premises: Dockhorn (review of Wahrheit und Methode) reads Luther's Affektenlehre as the secret history of the hermeneutics of facticity
Luther's Tischreden formula: 'Dialectica docet, Rhetorica movet'
Luther recognized that without affect, the past Passion of Christ would remain intangible and the future fear of God's wrath abstract
Heidegger secularizes this in SS 1924: 'we are moved ultimately not by fantasy, but by concrete possibilities contoured by experience'
Therefore Heidegger's pathos doctrine has a specifically Lutheran-rhetorical-theological lineage
targets: Reading Heidegger's pathos doctrine as purely Aristotelian without Christian-theological mediation
The Roman-tradition fantasy account of pathos-via-phantasia

section_4_main_positions.claim: In SS 1924, Heidegger's reading of Aristotle's Rhetoric and Politics produces a 'rhetorical pluralism' (proto-Arendtian): 'The determination of Being-with-one-another in politikē founds that which rhetoric brings to language' (GA 18 127); humans have political existence (bios politikos) only as their actions are coordinated in a common world; ethics shows how Being-in-the-world is differentiated, rhetoric how Dasein's articulations are situated in time and place. This is the Heidegger Arendt would later claim as the antidote to Heideggerian politics.
premises: GA 18 127: politikē grounds rhetoric, not the reverse
Authentic speaking emerges only from political community (per Gross's reading of Aristotle's corpus through Heidegger)
Without pathos and the political coordination it presupposes, community would remain mute
Therefore SS 1924 is genuinely pluralist-political-rhetorical, anticipating Arendt's political philosophy
targets: Reading Heidegger 1924 in the light of Heidegger 1933 (anachronism backwards)
Heidegger's later (post-1933) anti-Arendtian moves

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's hermeneutic turn between SS 1924 and Being and Time (1927) — the substitution of Befindlichkeit for the explicit rhetorical-pathos vocabulary — entailed dropping his earlier convictions that public speaking could authentically emerge from political community and that such an emergence would be motivated by pathos. BT moves Heidegger 'decisively out of the emotional public sphere and into the rarefied domain of the resolute Freeman' (BT 434). The Roman compromise's logos-pathos split is partly reproduced in the BT distinction between authentic-resoluteness and inauthentic-Mitsein.
premises: BT 238: ethics reconstructed via primordial care, ordinary phenomena 'drop out'
BT 344: only resolute Being-their-Selves enables authentic Being-with — collapse of pre-resolute political community
BT 159: only half-hearted suggestion of authentic Being-with through devotion to 'the same affair in common'
BT 434: rarefied domain of the resolute Freeman replaces emotional public sphere
Hermeneutic method penetrates to formal-universal level of Being; Aristotelian triad of politics-ethics-rhetoric becomes 'derivative social phenomena'
Therefore BT's hermeneutic turn coincides with the depoliticization of Heidegger's rhetorical thinking
targets: Continuity-readings that take SS 1924 → BT as smooth genetic line (Kisiel's general genetic thesis is acknowledged but Gross flags the substantive cost)
Readings that see Befindlichkeit as full-equivalent of pathos

section_4_main_positions.claim: Heidegger's 1933 turn (Rectoral Address, support for Hitler, withdrawal-from-League-of-Nations rhetoric, adherence to the German Führer) is not a contingent biographical lapse but the political-philosophical *consequence* of having lost (between 1924 and 1933) the rhetorical-political resources he himself discovered in SS 1924. Heidegger's 1930s reading of Nietzsche on great-passion-as-self-composed-superiority-of-great-will (Heidegger Nietzsche I 48-49) shows the body politic subordinated to 'the so-called great will' — the rhetorical pluralism of 1924 is gone.
premises: 1924 Heidegger: rhetorical pluralism, pathos as ontological substrate of community
1933 Heidegger: 'resolute Freeman' → 'resolute nation,' adherence to the German Führer
1930s Heidegger on Nietzsche: passion 'displays the self-composed superiority characteristic of great will' (italics added by Gross)
The shift from rhetorical-pluralism to great-will-superiority is the rhetorical/political consequence of the hermeneutic turn
Therefore Heidegger's Nazism has rhetorical-philosophical roots traceable to the BT-era abandonment of his SS 1924 commitments
targets: Apologetic readings that quarantine Heidegger's 1933 from his philosophy proper
Readings that treat 1933 as wholly contingent or biographical
Pöggeler's restricted-rhetoric-thesis insofar as it would deny rhetorical-political continuity is at issue

section_4_main_positions.claim: After SS 1924, rhetoric is depoliticized: the rhetorical responsibility for understanding 'what one did in speaking and what changes in the world one could thereby effect' is handed off — locutions to grammarians, legalities to logicians, the residue ('illocutionary' / 'perlocutionary') to philosophers of language (Grice, Searle, Habermas, Sperber). This twentieth-century pragmatic-philosophy outsourcing of rhetorical responsibility 'sweeps' power into 'amorphous backgrounds' of unarticulated predispositions. The volume's titular project ('rhetorical ontology') is the recovery work this depoliticization makes necessary.
premises: Modern speech-act theory analyzes context but as 'unevaluated background of unarticulated predispositions'
Rhetoric's classical political-ethical-emotional context-formation work is left unaccounted
Power becomes 'manifest in discursive histories' but invisible to the analytic apparatus
Therefore the analytic-pragmatic tradition has lost what early Heidegger had in 1924
targets: Speech-act theory as it stands (Grice, Searle, Habermas, Sperber) — too thin to recover what was lost
Apolitical philosophy of language
The 'amorphous background' move in pragmatics

section_5_interlocutors.name: Aristotle
section_5_interlocutors.role: Primary text. Two Aristotles in tension: (a) Rhetoric I.1 (1354a) where Aristotle dismisses pathos as 'making the rule crooked'; (b) Rhetoric II where pathē are condition of judgment (krisis). Heidegger reads Aristotle II against Aristotle I via GA 18; Gross extends this. Aristotle Rhetoric II.5 phobos definition is structurally central. Aristotle Politics provides bios politikos as context for rhetorical pluralism. Aristotle Rhetoric chapters on three modes of persuasion (ethos/pathos/logos) and the typology of fearsome people (Rhet 1382a30 area, nine kinds in three categories).
citations: Rhetoric 1354a (Rhet. I.1 — straightedge analogy, Aristotle dismissing pathos)
Rhetoric II generally (pathē as condition of krisis — book p. 30, GA 18 169 quote)
Rhetoric 1382a20 area (phobos definition — Heidegger's discussion in GA 18)
Rhetoric II.5 typology of fearsome people (book p. 36-37 — three categories: ill-disposed, advantage-seekers, cowardly)
Politics (bios politikos = political animal as basis for rhetorical pluralism, book p. 40)
section_5_interlocutors.relationship: Primary text Heidegger (and Gross via Heidegger) read; Aristotle's Rhetoric II is the rhetorical-ontological canon

section_5_interlocutors.name: Plato
section_5_interlocutors.role: Negative foil. Plato's Gorgias diatribe against rhetoric (459c — sophistic technique) is the founding moment of the philosophical caution toward pathos. Gross reads this caution itself as 'the symptom of a profoundly divisive political philosophy separating experts from the masses.' Plato is the original locus of the rationalist anti-pathos prejudice Heidegger will later overturn through Aristotle Rhetoric II.
citations: Gorgias 459c (book p. 27)
section_5_interlocutors.relationship: Critiqued — as origin of the philosophical anti-rhetorical prejudice

section_5_interlocutors.name: Cicero
section_5_interlocutors.role: Roman compromise. Cicero in De inventione, De oratore (esp. through the character Antonius and Catulus, 2.44.186-187, 2.52.214). Cicero is presented as the inaugural Roman 'add pathos to logos by sheer fiat' move — the pragmatic-but-suspect compromise. The citation 'wisdom in itself is silent and powerless to speak ... ratio atque oratio' (De inventione opening) is given as the compromise's strongest formulation. Cicero is also the source of the seduction-to-aggression slippery-slope worry about emotional manipulation.
citations: De inventione (opening — ratio atque oratio formulation)
De oratore 2.44.186-187 (Antonius's passionate-style speech)
De oratore 2.52.214 (passionate vs. dry speakers)
De oratore 2.44.189 (the orator visibly stamped with the emotion)
section_5_interlocutors.relationship: Critiqued — exemplifies the Roman compromise Heidegger rejects

section_5_interlocutors.name: Quintilian
section_5_interlocutors.role: Roman compromise (continued). Institutio oratoria 6.1.7 ('appeals to emotion are necessary if there are no other means for securing the victory of truth, justice and the public interest') and 6.2.29 (phantasia) are the two structurally central passages. Quintilian's reluctant-defense framing — pathos as concession to flawed humanity — is the canonical statement of pathos-as-supplement. Quintilian's example of imagining a murder scenario (6.2.31) is the Roman fantasy-model Heidegger reverses.
citations: Institutio oratoria 6.1.7 (reluctant defense)
Institutio oratoria 6.2.29 (phantasia definition)
Institutio oratoria 6.2.31 (murder-scenario example)
section_5_interlocutors.relationship: Critiqued — Roman fantasy-model is what Heidegger reverses (individual mentation as product of passion, not its source)

section_5_interlocutors.name: Martin Luther
section_5_interlocutors.role: The Affektenlehre tradition's culmination. Luther's Sermo de poenitentia and Tischreden are the structurally central texts. Per Dockhorn, Luther's principle 'Belief realizes itself in affect — must complete itself in affect — because reason is incapable of making past and future present' grounds the Enlightenment's rhetorical-theological subterranean tradition. Luther's Tischreden formula 'Dialectica docet, Rhetorica movet' is the rhetorical-theological seed of Heidegger's pathos doctrine. Luther recognized that without affect, the past Passion of Christ would remain intangible.

As Heidegger describes it, doxa reveals authentic being-with-one-another in the world ("Die doxa ist die eigentliche Entdecktheit des Miteinanderseins-in-der-Welt" [149]).' Gross gives the German verbatim. This is the rhetorical-ontological core: doxa is not opinion but disclosedness-of-being-with.

section_6_heidegger_loci.section_or_para: Pathos as Umschlagen / Werden zu / hexis
section_6_heidegger_loci.context_in_essay: Long English-and-German parallel block-quote (book pp. 35-36): English on p. 35: 'Pathos is a sudden change and hence a transformation to ... out of a previous situation, but not a sudden change that would take its own course. Instead, it is a way of disposing oneself toward the world that stands at the same time in a possible relation to hexis. This change into another condition and the new being composed from the old has in itself for the possibility of being-seized, being-suddenly-overcome. This way of losing composure, being-made-to-lose-composure, is done in such a way that composure can be regained; I can compose myself again. I am in danger at a particular moment, in a moment of terror, composed. I can draw to this disposition through the condition marked by terror by way of a possible being-composed-for.' German on p. 36 (verbatim): '[Pathos ist ein "Umschlagen" und demnach ein bestimmtes "Werden zu ..." aus einer früheren Lage, aber nicht ein Umschlagen, das für sich einen eigenen Verlauf hätte, sondern eine Weise des Sichbefindens in der Welt, die zugleich in einem möglichen Bezug steht zur hexis. Dieses Umschlagen in eine andere Verfassung und das Sein in der neuen von der alten her hat in sich selbst die Möglichkeit des Ergriffenwerdens, Überfallenwerdens. Die Art und Weise des Aus-der-Fassung-Kommens, Aus-der-Fassung-gebracht Werdens ist dem Sinn nach so, daß sie wieder gefaßt werden kann; Ich kann mich wieder fassen, ich bin in einem bestimmten Moment, in einer Gefahr, im Moment des Schreckens, in Fassung. Ich kann die durch den Schrecken gekennzeichnete Befindlichkeit beziehen auf ein mögliches Gefaßtsein dafür (171).]' This is the volume's most-cited Heidegger pathos definition.

section_8_tensions_open_questions.description: Pathos as Aristotelian recovery vs. pathos as Lutheran-theological inheritance. Gross holds both: pathos is Heidegger's reading of Rhetoric II (the Aristotelian recovery), AND pathos is mediated through Luther's Affektenlehre via Dockhorn (the theological-rhetorical genealogy). [INTERP-low]: Gross does not fully reconcile whether the Aristotelian recovery requires the Lutheran mediation or whether the Lutheran tradition is a subterranean parallel; the lateral framing 'Heidegger's analysis of fear ... clearly draws on this Lutheran tradition while rewriting its residual metaphysics' (book p. 34) suggests the latter, but the two strands are never fully integrated.

Continuity vs. rupture between SS 1924 and BT (intra-Heidegger). On one hand Gross affirms a genetic line (relying on Kisiel) — SS 1924 is where 'this discovery was made public for the first time' (book p. 27); on the other, BT 'dropped his convictions that public speaking could authentically emerge from political community' (book p. 40). Befindlichkeit replaces pathē but with conceptual loss. [INTERP-low]: Gross navigates this tension by distinguishing genetic continuity (yes, BT inherits SS 1924) from substantive continuity (no, BT loses the rhetorical-political dimension); whether this distinction is sustainable is a live question.

Pathos as ontological substrate (Gross HR-01-GROSS-B-P1) vs. pathos as cognitive-rhetorical resource (Hyde HR-04-HYDE on epideictic). VT5 of phase0. Gross dissolves the orator into pre-cognitive Befindlichkeit; Hyde retains the orator's intentional structure. Both cite GA 18 §§ on pathē. The ontological-substrate reading and the cognitive-resource reading are not obviously compatible registers.

Rhetoric central (Gross) vs. rhetoric restricted (Pöggeler). VT1 of phase0. Section IV's title 'The Priority of Pathos' implicitly states the volume's strongest centralization claim; Pöggeler Ch 7 takes the opposite view. Gross's depoliticization-by-hermeneutics thesis (book p. 41) actually predicts Pöggeler's view as a *symptom* of Heidegger's post-1924 trajectory — Pöggeler reads the late Heidegger and finds rhetoric restricted; Gross reads the early Heidegger and explains why the late Heidegger looks restricted.

VT11 of phase0: BT pipeline records Befindlichkeit (BT D1 U5, §§29-30) as central; HR pipeline records the pathos genealogy. Gross argues pathos does conceptual work BT *conceals* with the term Befindlichkeit. The BT German appendix reads Befindlichkeit as the canonical equivalent; HR-01-GROSS-B-P8 argues it is a substantive narrowing. Phase 3D cross-link will need to flag this productive tension.

The political ascription move. Gross treats the 1933 turn as politically-philosophically *consequent* on the BT-era depoliticization (P9). But Section IV does not provide a tight syllogism — the leap from 'BT depoliticizes rhetoric' to '1933 follows' is mediated by the 1930s Nietzsche reading (Heidegger Nietzsche I 48-49) and Heidegger's 1933 speeches. [INTERP-low]: The argument is suggestive, not deductive. Whether the Nietzsche-reading is *necessary* for the 1933 turn or one *symptom* among others is left underdetermined; the essay assumes (without arguing) that the same theoretical disposition that abandons rhetorical-pluralism also predisposes toward great-will politics.

The Ja-sagen-without-examination paradox. Doxa is characterized by Ja-sagen, kein Untersuchen, Reflektieren (book p. 31, GA 18 136-137). But doxa is also explicitly the openness of 'Es könnte auch anders sein' and the ground of articulation. [INTERP-low]: How yes-saying-without-examination can simultaneously be openness-to-revision is a structural question Gross sidesteps. The implicit answer (doxa is provisionally fixed AND structurally revisable, like a hexis with built-in temporality) is not unpacked.

The Bröcker vs. Schalk transcript variant at GA 18 110 (Note 1). Michalski (volume Ch 3 contributor and GA 18 editor) follows Schalk's 'aristotelischen Logic' reading; Gross follows Bröcker's 'aristotelischen Rhetorik' reading. The variant is conceptually important: 'forgetting to ask about the concrete function of Aristotelian Rhetoric/Logic' is a different claim. Gross flags this against the volume's editorial machinery.

section_10_edges.note: Gross's signature thesis: pathos is the ground that explains logos's possibility. Pathē 'compose ... the ground upon which language grows and to which expressions return' (GA 18 262, book p. 38).

Stronger ontological direction: logos presupposes pathos (not the reverse). Per Heidegger GA 18 169: 'with the demonstration of the fundamental role that the pathē play in krinein, we realize at the same time the possibility of seeing more concretely the ground of logos itself.'

Per GA 18 151 (HR-01-GROSS-B-HL5): 'doxa is set out as the ground and motive [Boden, Quelle und Antrieb] for speaking-with-one-another, negotiating-with-one-another.' Doxa IS what Mitanderreden means rhetorical-ontologically.

Per GA 18 261 (HR-01-GROSS-B-HL13): 'Wenn uns unheimlich ist, fangen wir an zu reden ... das Sprechen zusammenhängt mit der Grundbestimmung des Daseins.' Fear is the Befindlichkeit that brings into speech — the daseinsmäßige genesis of speaking.

Per GA 18 171 (HR-01-GROSS-B-HL7): pathos as Umschlagen 'stands at the same time in a possible relation to hexis' — pathos is the dynamic-pole of which hexis is the settled-pole. Pathos and hexis are paired structural moments of disposition.

Per GA 18 122 (HR-01-GROSS-B-HL2): 'Diese pathē, "Affekte" sind nicht Zustände des Seelischen, es handelt sich um eine Befindlichkeit des Lebenden in seiner Welt' — affects are NOT psychological states, they ARE Befindlichkeit. Identification, not equivalence.

But Gross argues BT's Befindlichkeit *narrows* the GA 18 pathos: BT 344 confines authentic Mitsein to resoluteness, BT 434 moves into 'rarefied domain of resolute Freeman.' So Befindlichkeit is identified with pathos in 1924 (HL2) but conceptually shrinks the political-rhetorical content by the time of BT.

Cicero/Quintilian's 'add pathos to logos by sheer fiat' (book p. 29) is exactly what Heidegger rejects. The Roman compromise is a posteriori contingent; the GA 18 pathos-priority is constitutive a priori.

Quintilian Inst. or. 6.2.29: passions as products of phantasia (individual mentation imagining the absent). Heidegger reverses: 'Passions are the product of individual mentation. Heidegger reverses this scheme, arguing that in fact individual mentation is the product of passion' (book p. 35).

Per Dockhorn (and Gross): Luther's Affektenlehre 'grounds Enlightenment philosophy, opening the way for what would later become the hermeneutics of facticity practiced by both Heidegger and Gadamer' (book p. 34). Genealogical link: medieval theology → Luther → Dockhorn-recognized substrate of hermeneutics-of-facticity.

Gross's depoliticization-by-hermeneutics thesis (P10) provides the philosophical mechanism by which the rhetorical-pluralist 1924 Heidegger can become the 1933 Heidegger (P9). P10 explains how P9 becomes possible.

VT5 cross-essay tension: Gross treats pathos as ontological substrate (the orator dissolved into pre-cognitive Befindlichkeit); Hyde keeps pathos as cognitive-rhetorical resource (the orator's intentional structure preserved in epideictic). Both cite GA 18 §§ on pathē. The two readings are likely not seamlessly compatible.

VT1 cross-essay tension: Gross's depoliticization-by-hermeneutics thesis predicts Pöggeler's titular 'restricted conception' as a *symptom* of Heidegger's post-1924 trajectory. Gross reads early Heidegger and explains why the late Heidegger looks restricted; Pöggeler reads late Heidegger and finds restriction. Cross-essay relation is not opposition but explanatory complementarity (Gross provides the genetic story for what Pöggeler observes synchronically).

Gross's 'rhetorical pluralism of 1924' thesis (P7) supports Kisiel's 'rhetorical protopolitics' thesis (HR-06). Both argue SS 1924 is the locus of an explicit political-rhetorical Heidegger that the later Heidegger leaves behind. Kisiel adds the three-phase model (Phenomenological / Metontological / Archaic-Poietic); Gross focuses on the loss in the BT transition.

Cross-essay support: Gross's pathos-as-ground thesis (P1) supports Struever's 'rhetoric as life-science' / Alltäglichkeit-as-temporality thesis. Both read SS 1924 as the locus where rhetoric becomes constitutive (not derivative) of Dasein's everyday self-articulation. Struever's Ch 5 epigraph (GA 18 110) parallels Gross's reading of GA 18 110-127.

Heidegger GA 18 262 ('the pathē are the ground upon which language grows and to which expressions return') operationalizes Aristotle's Rhetoric II treatment of pathē as condition of judgment. The relation is from Heidegger's German philosophical formulation back to Aristotle's Greek rhetorical-treatise framework.

GA 18 169 ('with the demonstration of the fundamental role that the pathē play in krinein, we realize at the same time the possibility of seeing more concretely the ground of logos itself') is Heidegger's programmatic statement of how he will read Aristotle Rhet II — pathē-in-krinein as access to the ground of logos.

Heidegger GA 18 256-257 (Aristotle's nine-types-of-fearsome-people in three categories) operationalizes Aristotle Rhetoric II.5's phobos definition (1382a20-1382b3) — turning it from a rhetorical-typological list into a relational-temporal-modal Befindlichkeit analysis.

GA 18 171's pathos-as-Umschlagen formulation refines Aristotle's Rhetoric II account by adding the modal-ontological dimension (pathos has the structure of being-able-to-recover-composure / Gefaßtsein dafür). This is Heidegger's distinctive philosophical addition to Aristotle's rhetorical analysis.

Heidegger GA 18 127 ('the determination of Being-with-one-another in politikē founds that which rhetoric brings to language') operationalizes Aristotle's Politics I's bios politikos / zoon politikon / koinonia framework — the politicality of human existence is what grounds the rhetorical capacity.

BT 178 (the explicit footnote citation) reads Aristotle's Rhetoric II as the 'first systematic hermeneutic of the everydayness of Being-with-one-another.' This BT formulation IS Heidegger's published self-statement of what Aristotle Rhetoric II ontologically means.

BT 344 ('only authentically Being-their-Selves in resoluteness can people authentically be with one another') contrasts with GA 18 127 ('determination of Being-with-one-another in politikē'): BT narrows authentic Mitsein to individual resoluteness, while SS 1924 grounded Miteinandersein in politikē. Same authority (Heidegger) speaking against itself across three years; this is the substantive shift Gross diagnoses.

BT 434 ('rarefied domain of the resolute Freeman') is the canonical pinpoint of the depoliticization. The phrase exemplifies the hermeneutic-turn's withdrawal from emotional public sphere into formal-individual resoluteness.

Per Dockhorn (note 48): 'Time and again, in Luther's Tischreden in particular, we hit upon the formula "Dialectica docet, Rhetorica movet." And Luther knows exactly what he means by the movere of rhetoric.' Luther's rhetorical-theological formula is the historical seed of Heidegger's pathos-as-grounding-logos. Genealogical, not just analogical.

Engberg-Pedersen exemplifies the apologetic-condescending Aristotle-rhetoric reading Gross attacks (book p. 30): 'pathos is regrettably necessary' — the very prejudice Gross's priority-of-pathos thesis dismantles. The undermining runs both directions: Gross's P1 also undermines Engberg-Pedersen.

Gross's depoliticization thesis (P10) sharply undermines modern speech-act theory's adequacy: Searle/Grice/Habermas/Sperber analyze illocutionary/perlocutionary dimensions but with no political-ethical-rhetorical context — only an 'unevaluated background of unarticulated predispositions.' The result is power-becoming-invisible-to-the-analytic-apparatus.

Gross's bold thesis: Heidegger's 1933 (Nazism) is the political consequence of the depoliticization. The 1933 'resolute Freeman → resolute nation → German Führer' progression and the 1930s Nietzsche-reading on great-will exemplify the hermeneutic turn's loss of rhetorical-political resources. NOT a strict syllogism but a structural ascription.

The volume's titular 'rhetorical ontology' project (Gross's positive proposal) presupposes the depoliticization diagnosis (P10): only because rhetoric was depoliticized in the hermeneutic turn does the recovery work of 'rhetorical ontology' need to be done. The positive project requires the negative diagnosis.
